title: On effects of composition and single and double annealing of medium-manganese steels for hot press forming: a review
abstract: Abstract Recent breakthroughs in medium-manganese steels have redefined paradigms for metastable austenite engineering in advanced high-strength steels. The present contribution elucidates the thermodynamic and kinetic principles governing microstructure evolution during intercritical annealing and subsequent hot/warm forming. Particular attention is given to steel processing, highlighting how double annealing and hot/warm stamping can tailor mechanical properties (e.g., achieving 1000 MPa of tensile strength with 35% total elongation) through controlled austenite retention. Emerging evidence suggests that strain-induced martensite transformation kinetics during stamping are critically dependent on prior austenite grain morphology—a relationship requiring further atomistic investigation. The discussion analyses different roadmaps for implementing medium-Mn steels for various components in the automotive body-in-white, requiring different properties. It also identifies unresolved questions regarding how the chemistry of the steel, in addition to the processing parameters, influences the retained austenite fraction and its impact on the tensile properties.
journal: Journal of Iron and Steel Research International

sections.heading: Introduction
paragraphs: The automotive industry has been continually dealing with the challenges of reducing car fuel consumption to limit greenhouse gas emissions while meeting the constantly increasing safety requirements, especially by improving the crashworthiness of the automobile structure. Consequently, current research on automotive steels aims to develop new steel grades with a higher strength–ductility combination or to improve the existing grades for lightweight automobiles through the implementation of different heat treatments, ensuring passenger safety effectively [ 1 ,  2 ]. The car body structure combines two main types of components: anti-intrusion type, the components that react to loads with minimal deformation (most of them in the safety cell), and energy-absorbing type, the ones that deform under load to absorb energy [ 3 ]. The effective use of these components depends not only on their high-strength levels but also on formability. Moreover, the numerous socio-economic, geopolitical, and technological challenges have led to a new way of thinking about the design of vehicles and components, primarily focused on weight reduction by using materials with high specific strength, lower density or higher Young’s modulus [ 4 ,  5 ,  6 – 7 ]. Therefore, new steels must be characterized by their high strength, while not neglecting formability, weldability, toughness, stretch flangeability, hydrogen embrittlement, fatigue resistance, density, stiffness, etc. Currently, three generations of advanced high-strength steels (AHSS) have been developed and have evolved to increase the stiffness of the high-strength steel sheets used for automobile body structures, leading to reductions in sheet thickness and thus mass reductions [ 8 ,  9 ]. First-generation AHSS is a term that includes conventional C–Mn steels and the most well-known grades, such as transformation-induced plasticity (TRIP), dual phase (DP), complex phase (CP), and martensitic (MART) steels. Examples of the second generation of AHSS are the high-Mn austenitic steels with twinning-induced plasticity (TWIP), austenitic stainless steels, and the lightweight steels with induced plasticity (L-IP). As shown in Fig.  1 , they display mechanical properties of great interest for automotive applications, but with a high production cost due to the high alloying additions and the strict manufacturing processes required to obtain austenitic microstructures, making them unaffordable for large-scale production. Third-generation AHSS for the automotive industry combines the benefits of multiphase structures with the hardening-enhancing mechanisms of the austenitic phase (mechanical twinning and strain-induced martensitic transformation) [ 10 ,  11 – 12 ]. Fig. 1 Total elongation versus ultimate tensile strength for different sheet steels: interstitial-free (IF) steel, interstitial-free high-strength (IF–HS) steel, isotropic (ISO) steel, bake-hardening (BH) steel, C-Mn (C–Mn) steel, high-strength low-alloy (HSLA) steel, ferrite-bainite (FB) steel, DP steel, CP steel, TRIP steel, Mn-boron steel used in press-hardened parts (MnB + HPF steel), MART steel, quenching and partitioning (Q&P) steel, complex phase with bainite and ferrite (CBF) steel, L-IP steel, TWIP steel [ 13 ,  14 ,  15 – 16 ]

Worldwide, automotive regulations demand a reduction of CO 2  emissions, not only for the in-use cars but also for the automakers’ processes, leading to the development of strategies for weight reductions in cars without cutbacks in crash performance [ 17 ,  18 ,  19 – 20 ]. Steel grades with high yield and ultimate tensile strengths have been used in the manufacture of lighter and more rigid anti-intrusion components for auto bodies with no reduction of crash performance [ 21 ,  22 – 23 ]. Hot forming is a well-known process used to manufacture complex-shaped high-strength parts for automobiles since 1984 [ 24 ]. During hot forming, parts are formed at high temperatures (thereby improving their formability) and then cooled at a fast rate to strengthen the steel [ 25 ,  26 ], also reducing the springback [ 27 ]. Hot-formed parts constitute more than 30% of the steel in many automobile body models used in the market [ 28 ,  29 ].

This review discusses the advancements and key features of single annealing and double annealing of medium-Mn steels on their microstructural evolution and mechanical properties, which make them suitable for use in automotive components. The double annealing is also in the context of hot press forming of medium-Mn steels because after the final annealing of the cold-rolled steels at the steelmakers, the thermal cycles applied during hot press forming can be constructed as a second annealing. Therefore, a brief review of hot press forming of medium-Mn steels is also presented, elucidating the effects of various parameters of the hot-forming process, as well as the paint baking step following hot press forming.

sections.heading: Composition effects of alloying elements
paragraphs: The typical medium-Mn steels contain, in addition to Mn, C, Si, Al, covering a wide range of chemical compositions; moreover, the addition of chromium and other minor alloying additions such as V, Ti, Nb, Mo, and Ni are also reported [ 59 ,  60 ,  61 ,  62 – 63 ]. Since the final properties of medium-Mn steels depend on complex interactions between alloying elements, metallurgical and technological processes and their parameters, it appears challenging to describe a univocal effect of a specific element. However, the main effects of the individual alloying elements are summarized in the following.

sections.heading: Manganese
paragraphs: In the context of medium-Mn steels, the term typically denotes steels with manganese (Mn) contents ranging from 3 to 12 wt.% [ 15 ]. Mn acts as a crucial phase stabilizer in these alloys, playing a pivotal role throughout the entire steelmaking process and influencing solid-state phase transformations. Consequently, Mn significantly affects the phase constituents, including volume fractions and microstructural features, thereby ultimately affecting the mechanical properties derived from thermomechanical treatments applied to these grades.

The exceptional mechanical performance of medium-Mn steels is predominantly linked to deformation- and stress-induced phase transformations, notably the TRIP effect. Mn exerts a significant influence on the stacking fault energy (SFE), a critical parameter governing phase stability. The martensitic transformation of metastable retained austenite embedded within the microstructure leads to increased work hardening and localized strengthening, particularly in the necking zone. This mechanism suppresses localized deformation, delaying necking onset and thereby achieving an excellent balance between strength and ductility through concurrent improvement in ultimate tensile strength (UTS) and uniform elongation (UE) [ 8 ,  35 ,  37 ]. Consequently, higher retained austenite fractions—attainable by increased Mn content—are essential for optimizing these properties [ 69 ,  75 ,  76 ].

Regarding the interplay between SFE and the TRIP effect, deformation generates favorable nucleation sites for martensite, offsetting the low chemical driving force and facilitating martensitic transformation via stress-assisted (SAMT) or strain-induced mechanisms (SIMT) [ 77 ]. Activation of the TRIP effect typically requires an SFE below 20 mJ/m 2  [ 78 ]. Mn additions elevate the SFE beyond this threshold, potentially promoting TWIP at approximately 20 mJ/m 2  [ 54 ,  78 ,  79 ]. The relationship between Mn content and SFE exhibits a parabolic trend: initially decreasing with increasing Mn concentrations but rising for contents exceeding 12 wt.%. Notably, within the medium-Mn range (3–12 wt.%) and assuming constant levels of other alloying elements, Mn incrementally reduces SFE, as is reported by Zambrano [ 80 ] and by Lee and Choi [ 81 ].

In addition, Mn significantly enhances solid-solution strengthening, exhibiting an estimated strengthening coefficient of 44.5 MPa per wt.% Mn. This effect is further supported by the inherently low diffusivity of Mn within the austenitic matrix [ 54 ]. The latter promotes the formation of heterogeneous microstructures characterized by mechanical stability gradients, which play a key role in optimizing the overall mechanical performance of the material [ 14 ,  15 ,  57 ]. Furthermore, increased Mn content expedites the kinetics of austenite reversion—an issue discussed in detail in a subsequent section—thereby enabling reduced annealing and hot-forming dwell times [ 30 ,  82 ,  83 ].

sections.heading: Carbon
paragraphs: According to Mola et al. [ 87 ], a high carbon content accelerates the precipitation of cementite, particularly at grain boundaries. This promotes premature fracture during tensile loading, typically occurring without necking and leading to a reduction in total elongation.

An increase in carbon content beyond 0.1 wt.% in medium-Mn steels adversely affects their weldability by promoting crack formation in the heat-affected zone (HAZ). Additionally, elevated carbon levels can reduce formability, which is detrimental to automotive manufacturing processes such as deep drawing and stamping [ 21 ,  88 ]. In medium-Mn steels, the carbon content is typically controlled between 0.05 and 0.07 wt.% to optimize formability for complex geometries, whereas a carbon concentration of 0.08–0.1 wt.% enhances the strength while maintaining sufficient ductility necessary for the fabrication of safety-critical components [ 89 ,  90 – 91 ].

sections.heading: Aluminum
Silicon
Chromium
Titanium
paragraphs: Medium-Mn steels frequently utilize various microalloying elements—such as Ti, V, and Nb—to enhance strength and ductility, primarily via mechanisms including grain refinement, precipitation strengthening, and adjustments to phase fractions achieved by modifying the matrix carbon content [ 121 ]. The specific roles of V and Nb will be addressed in subsequent sections. With regard to Ti, it is commonly introduced at concentrations up to 0.15 wt.% [ 121 ]. Due to the higher cost of Nb and V, Ti is increasingly considered a more economically attractive alternative.

Regarding tensile properties, the same study reported that increasing Ti from 0.014 to 0.032 wt.% resulted in a 140 MPa increase in yield strength, attributable to the combined effects of precipitation hardening by TiC and grain refinement. However, further increasing the Ti content to 0.053 wt.% was found to be detrimental, as it significantly reduced the mechanical stability of the reverted austenite, thereby lowering elongation and impact toughness.

sections.heading: Niobium and vanadium
paragraphs: Vanadium (V), also a potent carbide former, exerts a comparable influence. Bi et al. [ 130 ] showed that in steels with a composition of 0.12C – 10Mn – 1.25Si – 1.6Al, varying the V content (0.05 and 0.5 wt.%) leads to the precipitation of V carbides, which consequently deplete the C content in austenite. These carbides significantly pin both dislocations and grain boundaries (see Fig.  6 ), thereby retarding the growth of austenite during intercritical annealing. During the intercritical annealing, cementite dissolves, leaving only the vanadium carbides, providing carbon for the growth of austenite. Therefore, when V is added, the growth of austenite is slower. As a result, in addition, the final volume fraction of austenite is substantially reduced [ 130 ]. High V variants are also characterized by higher dislocation densities compared to low vanadium medium-Mn steels (MMnS) [ 130 ]. Fig. 6 Mechanism of pinning by V carbides in steels containing 0.12C–10.0Mn–1.25Si–1.6Al (wt.%) with V contents of 0.05 wt.% (LV steel) and 0.5 wt.% (HV steel) [ 130 ]

Vanadium also plays a significant role in determining the mechanical behavior of MMnS. The dispersion of V-rich carbides effectively hinders dislocation mobility, leading to localized stress accumulation within ferrite. Once this stress surpasses a critical threshold, new dislocations are nucleated in austenite, thereby activating additional slip systems that relieve stress and promote dislocation motion as well as the TRIP effect. The overall resistance to dislocation movement is further enhanced with increasing V content.

According to Zhu et al. [ 128 ], the UTS of Fe – 0.28C – 9.33Mn – 2.6Al (wt.%) steel increases by 293 MPa with the addition of 0.2–0.3 wt.% V, and by 393 MPa when further alloyed with 0.03 wt.% Nb, without any significant reduction in ductility [ 131 ].
Additionally, vanadium influences dynamic strain aging (DSA), as it modifies both dislocation density and mobility, as well as the carbon content within austenite [ 130 ,  132 ].

sections.heading: Increased alloying content and manufacturability
paragraphs: Despite the numerous advantages of medium- and high-Mn steels in the automotive industry, their large-scale industrial production faces several challenges.

Firstly, manufacturing medium-Mn steels requires specialized liquid steelmaking processes to tightly control phosphorus, sulfur and nitrogen levels to minimize inclusions, particularly manganese sulfides (MnS) [ 133 ,  134 ,  135 ,  136 – 137 ].

Additionally, when high Al contents are present, specialized mold powders may be necessary to prevent adverse reactions with mold slag due to aluminum’s strong affinity for oxygen. These reactions can lead to problems such as increased friction, sticking, and uneven heat extraction during casting [ 138 ]. Moreover, the high strain hardening exhibited by these steels during cold rolling makes producing coils within conventional width ranges very challenging, increasing the risk of cracking at high reduction rates [ 133 ,  139 ,  140 ]. Consequently, minimizing alloying element concentrations is critical for ensuring cost-effective steel production.

Another significant limitation stems from the high typical manganese, silicon, and Al contents in medium-Mn steels. This adversely affects the galvanizing process critical for automotive sheet steels, as most are zinc-coated. These elements can selectively oxidize under the typical atmosphere used during galvanizing, hindering iron dissolution from the steel substrate. This iron dissolution is essential for reacting with Al dissolved in the molten zinc bath. The formation of the Fe 2 Al 5 Zn x  interfacial layer from this reaction is crucial for achieving a defect-free coating with strong adhesion and good formability [ 141 ].

sections.heading: Microstructure evolution and austenite reversion transformation
paragraphs: Attempts to simplify or combine processing steps for greater energy and machinery efficiency are limited by technological challenges that impede industrial deployment. As detailed by Hu et al. [ 144 ], a novel route for Fe–0.2C–9.8Mn–3.5Al–1.2Si–0.29 V–0.0048N (wt.%) steel—bypassing hot rolling by reheating directly to an intercritical range before rolling—demonstrates enhanced mechanical performance. Nonetheless, large-scale industrial adoption is not currently possible due to: (1) dynamic phase transformations during rolling, leading to brittle martensite and compromised workability; (2) the need for precise strain and temperature control to avoid cementite precipitation and grain coarsening; (3) deformation-induced martensite in retained austenite, reducing ductility and increasing crack risk; and (4) disruption of manganese and carbon partitioning, causing unpredictable microstructural evolution.

sections.heading: Transformation mechanism
Effects of annealing temperature
Effects of annealing time
paragraphs: Jang et al. [ 57 ] reported the effect of multiple combinations of IA temperature and times on a 0.12C–5.8Mn–0.47Si–3.1Al (wt.%) containing steel. Their results are plotted in the radar chart of Fig.  12 , showing how different high-strength products with UTS between 850 and 1040 MPa and total elongation between 16.5% and 35.5% can be produced with only one steel chemistry. The achieved yield strength (YS) and RA contents are also shown in Fig.  12 . The TE increases with the RA content produced during the IA, with a relatively moderate reduction in the UTS. In addition, these steels provide robustness to product development in the automotive industry, producing steel sheets with a wide range of mechanical properties by changing only the annealing time and temperature to obtain high-strength and ultrahigh-strength, high-ductility steel products. Figure  13  illustrates the relationship between TE and UTS for numerous medium-Mn steels documented in the literature. The data reveal a relevant variability in mechanical properties even for steels with the same composition. In addition, the reported medium-Mn steels exhibit a broad distribution across the TE  vs.  UTS property space, highlighting the diverse processing–structure–property relationships available within them. Fig. 12 Radar chart correlating time and temperature of IA treatment with resulting tensile properties and RA fraction of a Fe–0.12C–5.8Mn–0.47Si–3.1Al (wt.%) steel [ 57 ] Fig. 13 TE versus UTS for different medium-Mn steels and their ESF after various IA treatments [ 55 ,  56 – 57 ,  59 ,  69 ,  94 ,  95 ,  101 ,  102 ,  106 ,  126 ,  153 ,  155 ,  159 ,  160 ,  161 – 162 ]

sections.heading: Microstructure evolution
Effects on mechanical properties
paragraphs: Ultra-low C steels with medium- or low-Mn additions exhibited a wide range of tensile properties depending on their processing, but at a strength level proportional to the added C, which limits their application for ultrahigh-strength hot-forming parts [ 176 ,  181 ]. Around 0.1 wt.% C is desirable to obtain a substantial amount of RA with no undesirable effect on the weldability. Also, adding some amount of Ni can help the RA stabilization and reduce the amount of required Mn. Si and Al additions aim to suppress the precipitation of cementite during tempering and contribute to solid strengthening at the same time [ 182 ,  183 – 184 ].

In Fig.  16 , the results obtained by Xu et al. [ 185 ] on a Fe–0.2C–4.72Mn (wt.%) steel are plotted, showing the effects of temperatures of first IA (FIA) and second IA (SIA) as independent parameters on the tensile properties. Firstly, they evaluated the FIA temperature to obtain a better UTS·TE value (Fig.  16 a), and then, that temperature was used to evaluate the effect of the SIA (Fig.  16 b). It is observed that medium-Mn steels have the potential to give several products for the automotive industry, with improved elongation due to the achievement of higher RA fractions, by changing the SIA temperature and time. Fig. 16 Radar chart correlating mechanical properties and RA fraction of a Fe–0.2C–4.72Mn (wt.%) steel.  a  Changing FIA temperature with constant SIA temperature, both for 30 min;  b  changing SIA temperature with former FIA temperature constant, both for 30 min [ 185 ]

Figure  17  demonstrates the influence of a double soaking treatment on the mechanical properties of a 0.14C–7.14Mn–0.23Si–0.056Al (wt.%) containing steel, initially subjected to a primary soak at 900 °C. The secondary annealing significantly changes the mechanical properties of the steel, by increasing the RA fraction and thereby enhancing TE at the expense of tensile strength. Notably, even under double soaking conditions that reduce strength by approximately 800 MPa, the steel achieves an optimal balance of ultrahigh strength with very high total elongation, with a UTS of ~ 1000 MPa and TE of 30%–40%, positioning it within the extra high-strength steel category while retaining exceptional formability. Fig. 17 Radar chart correlating time and temperature of DS treatment with resulting tensile properties and RA fraction of a medium-Mn steel containing 0.14C–7.14Mn in wt.% [ 179 ]

The plot in Fig.  18  shows the relationship of UTS·TE vs. the RA content of medium-Mn steels treated with double soaking found in the literature. As discussed before, the final properties depend not only on the chemistry but also on the previous treatment of steel. For this reason, the same trend of these parameters as in Fig.  11 c is observed, but at different values of UTS·TE and RA. The chemistry and annealing parameters of the steels plotted in Fig.  18  are listed in Table  1 . sections.heading: Effect of hot-press-forming process
paragraphs: Hot press forming (also known as hot stamping, press hardening, or simply hot forming) is a specialized method for producing automotive parts from sheet metal. In the most common type of hot forming, called direct hot forming, the process combines forming and die quenching in one step. This manufacturing method ensures precise dimensional control, high rigidity, and the ability to make complex geometrical shapes. Because of these benefits of hot forming, complex-shaped ultrahigh-strength parts for the automotive industry are widely produced with this technique. The commonly used steel grade for the purpose is 22MnB5 grade, which is also known as “boron steel.” As an example, Fig.  19  shows the usage of steel grades classified by their YS in the ID.4 electrical vehicle model of Volkswagen, in which hot-press-formed (i.e., form-hardened) parts are around 30% of the body-in-white [ 187 ]. Fig. 19 Steel body structure of Volkswagen ID.4 and its distribution of steel grades [ 187 ]

sections.heading: Reheating temperature
Reheating time
paragraphs: The reheating time to reach the maximum hardness (or strength) depends on the strip thickness and the reheating temperature [ 193 ]. First, the hardness of the steel strip increases sharply with the soaking time during the first minute, and then, it continues increasing but much more smoothly until a soaking time for the maximum hardness. In a 0.1C–5Mn–0.03Al (wt.%) containing steel with a thickness of 1.8 mm, the hardness increases from ~ 370 to ~ 450 HV after 60 s of reheating at 800 °C, increasing slightly with reheating time until 420 s, where it reaches a maximum value with a gain of only 20 HV (471 HV) [ 24 ]. Further heating leads to a hardness reduction because of grain coarsening [ 30 ].

sections.heading: Forming temperature
paragraphs: After reheating, the strip loses heat during transportation from the heating device to the stamping press. Studies on the optimal temperature to shape the steel have been done, establishing that the ideal temperature of forming is not the same as the optimal reheating temperature of the blanks, introducing then cooling devices between the furnace and press [ 196 ].

With increasing temperature, the strength of a medium-Mn steel was reported to decrease, which would facilitate low press forces, but the uniform elongation also decreased, raising concern that the high-temperature formability of medium-Mn steels may suffer [ 197 ]. However, Wróbel et al. [ 30 ] showed that the formability of medium-Mn steel rises gradually and then decreases with the forming temperature. The optimal forming temperature depends on several parameters, such as the steel chemistry, prior processing and its reflection on the microstructure before the hot forming. The best forming temperature lies between 200 and 300 °C below the reheating temperature. Chang et al. [ 30 ] reported an ideal forming temperature of around 450 °C for a Fe–5Mn–0.1C (wt.%) medium-Mn steel. The best forming temperature lies between 200 and 300 °C below the austenitization temperature. This is much lower than the ideal forming temperature for a 22MnB5 steel grade (700 °C) as reported by Zhao et al. [ 196 ].

sections.heading: Cooling rate
paragraphs: The cooling rate after forming is a key parameter for obtaining martensitic microstructures for the anti-intrusion components of auto bodies. High-speed phase transformation caused by high cooling rates induces significant residual stress, reducing the formability of the material. While cooling rates of a minimum of 27 °C/s are needed to obtain a fully martensitic microstructure in a 22MnB5 grade steel [ 65 ], Chang et al. [ 30 ] reported that a fully martensitic microstructure of a Fe–5Mn–0.1C (wt.%) medium-Mn steel can be obtained even at a cooling rate of 10 °C/s, but with lower tensile strength.

Chang et al. [ 30 ] concluded that the optimum parameters for warm stamping of a Fe–5Mn–0.1C (wt.%) medium-Mn steel are: (1) a reheating temperature between 790 and 840 °C with a holding time between 4 and 7 min and (2) an initial stamping temperature between 450 and 500 °C followed by a cooling rate between 10 and 60 °C/s, resulting in a great combination of high tensile strength and total elongation (1430–1460 MPa and 8%–11.5%, respectively).

sections.heading: Deformation degree
paragraphs: Although the hot-forming process inherently introduces varying degrees of deformation across different regions of a medium-Mn steel component, systematic studies quantifying the direct influence of deformation degree on mechanical properties remain scarce. The available literature typically evaluates properties at multiple positions on formed parts without specifying the corresponding local strains. Still, it consistently reports that mechanical properties such as tensile strength and ductility exhibit little variation across these zones (Fig.  20 ) [ 198 ,  199 ]. The lack of pronounced property gradients implies that medium-Mn steels may exhibit a relative insensitivity to deformation degree under typical hot-forming conditions. This robustness could be advantageous for automotive applications demanding uniform part performance, yet underscores the need for targeted experimental studies that accurately map strain and correlate it with microstructural evolution and mechanical response. Fig. 20 Tensile properties of hot-press-formed medium-Mn steel measured at various positions along B-pillar geometry [ 199 ]

sections.heading: Final properties
Paint baking
paragraphs: Paint baking (PB) or bake hardening is the low-temperature heating process (150–200 °C for around 20 min) that follows the hot press forming to give the automobile components its last required esthetic look [ 200 ]. This process bakes the paint on the automobile bodies-in-white and also cures and hardens adhesives and coatings [ 201 ,  202 ]. Pereloma and Timokhina [ 200 ] reported that PB induces an increase in the YS (around 10%), resulting in improved crash resistance and thus enabling a thickness reduction of the metal sheets used for the car body construction.

Moreover, PB affects the spot weldability of the material, which is a fundamental joining method of the automotive sector. As found by Eftekharimilani et al. [ 205 ], after PB the energy absorption capability of spot welds significantly increases without changing the failure mode, and hardness slightly decreases.

sections.heading: Future perspective
paragraphs: Emerging research directions should prioritize in situ characterization of microstructural evolution during thermomechanical processing. Synchrotron-based diffraction studies could elucidate real-time phase transformation kinetics under simulated stamping conditions, enabling predictive models for property optimization. The development of lean alloy variants with reduced processing steps—potentially through flash annealing techniques—may address cost barriers while maintaining performance.

To fully realize the potential of medium-Mn steels in next-generation vehicles, future work must bridge fundamental metallurgical insights with manufacturing realities. This requires coordinated efforts between computational materials design (leveraging machine learning for composition–processing–property predictions) and industrial validation through pilot–scale production trials. Such an integrated approach would position medium–Mn steels as a versatile materials platform capable of meeting competing demands for safety, efficiency and sustainability of the automotive industry.

Future research should prioritize a thorough investigation of the deformation behavior of medium-Mn steels during the hot-press-forming stage, which remains a critical and underexplored area. While studies have extensively characterized post-processing microstructures and mechanical properties, the in situ deformation mechanisms at elevated temperatures—particularly the complex interactions between thermal and mechanical effects—are not yet fully understood. The effects of key alloying elements such as manganese, carbon, aluminum, silicon, and vanadium on phase stability, dynamic recrystallization, and diffusion-controlled transformations during hot deformation require detailed examination. These elements influence the stability of retained austenite, martensite formation, and carbide precipitation, which in turn govern the mechanical response and microstructural evolution under hot-forming conditions. Developing comprehensive constitutive models and processing maps that account for both deformation parameters and chemical composition will be essential to optimize hot-forming processes. Addressing these challenges will be vital for enabling the reliable industrial application of medium-Mn steels in automotive manufacturing, where precise control of hot deformation can significantly enhance retained austenite stability and thereby improve tensile properties and formability.

sections.heading: Conclusions
paragraphs: This review summarizes key investigations on medium-Mn steels, focusing on the influence of composition, single and double annealing, and subsequent hot/warm stamping processes. By critically evaluating existing research, the present contribution highlights critical knowledge gaps, particularly concerning the specific metallurgical phenomena governing hot/warm stamping behavior.

The successful industrial application of hot/warm stamped medium-Mn steel components in the automotive sector hinges on precise control of processing parameters, ranging from alloy design to intercritical annealing and final forming conditions. Notably, the hot/warm stamping process offers exceptional versatility of mechanical properties through adjustments of secondary annealing time and temperature without additional modifications to the production line. This adaptability is crucial for manufacturing complex-shaped automotive body-in-white components with different properties while minimizing processing steps. Current advancements in medium-Mn steels and hot/warm stamping technologies thus provide direct and scalable solutions to meet the demand of the automotive industry for high-performance, lightweight, and cost-efficient materials.
